world_behind.title: The sermon has not changed subject
world_behind.text: Verse 1 says "I would cite your minds forward" and picks up the commandments of Alma 12. Rest, hardened hearts and the plan of redemption all carry over. What is new is that Alma now explains who was appointed to teach the thing he has been teaching, and on what basis.

world_behind.title: Melchizedek was thin in the record they had
world_behind.text: Genesis gives him three verses and no biography (Gen. 14:18–20). Alma supplies a reign, a wicked people, a preaching of repentance, a general repentance and the establishing of peace, and says of him that "none were greater" (v. 19). The brass plates evidently carried more of him than the Genesis that survived.

world_behind.title: Tithes are cited as the known fact
world_behind.text: Verse 15 offers Abraham's payment as the detail the hearers already have, and it is the one part of the Melchizedek story Genesis does keep. Alma builds the unfamiliar on the familiar.

world_behind.title: Salem was a city that repented
world_behind.text: This matters where it is being said. Alma is describing a wicked city whose people turned, standing in a wicked city that has about a year left. The parallel is offered without being pointed at.

world_behind.title: The chapter answers a question about fairness
world_behind.text: Verses 3 through 5 insist that those called were "on the same standing with their brethren" (v. 5) and were left in the first place to choose good or evil. Alma 9:6 has the men of Ammonihah demand who he is and by what authority he speaks, so ordination is being explained to people who have already challenged his standing to explain it to.

cites.quote: on the same standing with their brethren

spans.text: on the same standing with their brethren

world_behind.title: Angels are said to be at work right now
world_behind.text: Verse 24 claims angels are declaring the coming of Christ in their own land at that moment. Alma 8:14 has one meeting Alma on the road to this city and Alma 10:7 has one stopping Amulek on the way to a kinsman's house, both within the previous five chapters. The claim is offered as ordinary current events, and the reader has just watched two of them.

world_behind.title: The record notes what it did not keep
world_behind.text: Verse 31 says Alma spoke many more words that are not written. Two chapters earlier the same note closed Amulek's testimony. The book is repeatedly telling the reader that it is a selection.

words.text: Knowing beforehand. The word appears twice in this record and both times in this chapter, tying the calling of priests to what God knew before the world was. The King James Bible has it twice as well, once of Christ delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God (Acts 2:23), and once of the elect (1 Pet. 1:2). Alma is using a term the New Testament would later use for the same difficulty, and using it while insisting in the same breath that the men involved chose.

Loathing, a recoil at something disgusting. It occurs twice in this record and never in the King James Bible. The sanctified "could not look upon sin save it were with abhorrence" (v. 12). What it describes is a changed reflex. The claim is about what purity does to the sense of taste.

cites.quote: could not look upon sin save it were with abhorrence

spans.text: could not look upon sin save it were with abhorrence

words.text: A tenth part, paid. Alma gives the amount and the payer without explaining the practice, because Genesis already told his hearers that Abraham paid them to this same man (Gen. 14:20). The verse works as a citation: the one fact about Melchizedek the reader can check.

A pattern that points to something later. Treated at Mosiah 3:15. The ordinances were given so that people might look forward, "it being a type of his order" (v. 16), and Alma immediately corrects himself to say it is his order. The word lets him hold both at once: a resemblance and an identity.

cites.quote: it being a type of his order

spans.text: it being a type of his order

words.text: To twist, and in the King James Bible most often to twist a verdict. Exodus and Deuteronomy both forbid wresting judgment (Ex. 23:2; Deut. 16:19), and Peter uses it of the unlearned twisting scriptures to their own destruction (2 Pet. 3:16). Alma says "if ye will wrest them it shall be to your own destruction" (v. 20), and he says it to a city run by men whose profession is bending judgments. The warning arrives in their own trade word.

cites.quote: if ye will wrest them it shall be to your own destruction

spans.text: if ye will wrest them it shall be to your own destruction

words.text: To put off to tomorrow. Absent from the King James Bible, it enters this record here and returns once more, on Amulek's lips, twenty-one chapters later. Alma pairs it with the anxiety he says amounts to pain, so the word is doing emotional work as well as moral. The sin named is delay.

phrases.term: Called and prepared from the foundation of the world
phrases.text: The claim that sets up the whole chapter's difficulty. Preparation is placed before the world existed, and the next clause places a choice inside the same sentence. Alma does not resolve the tension. He states both halves and moves on.

phrases.term: In the first place being left to choose good or evil
phrases.text: The counterweight, supplied immediately. Whatever foreknowledge means here, it does not mean the men were spared the choosing. The phrase "in the first place" appears again two verses later, both times to insist that everyone started level.

phrases.term: They were on the same standing with their brethren
phrases.text: The fairness clause, and it is unusually direct. Nobody was given a head start. Those who were not called could have had "as great privilege as their brethren" (v. 4), and the verse names what intervened: hardness and blindness they chose.

cites.quote: as great privilege as their brethren

spans.text: as great privilege as their brethren

phrases.term: Without beginning of days or end of years
phrases.text: The phrase Hebrews uses of Melchizedek (Heb. 7:3), applied here to the order and not to the man. Alma will name Melchizedek eight verses later, so the borrowing is deliberate. What has no beginning in this account is an office.

phrases.term: Their garments were washed white through the blood of the Lamb
phrases.text: Washing white in blood is an image that ought not to work and does. It belongs to John's Revelation as well, and to Nephi before that. The sequence in the verse matters: called, then sanctified, then washed.

phrases.term: Could not look upon sin save it were with abhorrence
phrases.text: The chapter's description of holiness, phrased as an inability. These people are not resisting sin. They have lost the appetite. It is the most concrete thing said about sanctification anywhere in the sermon.

phrases.term: Bring forth fruit meet for repentance
phrases.text: John the Baptist's demand (Matt. 3:8), which Alma already used in its other form four chapters ago (Alma 9:30). Here it arrives as an invitation, and it is attached to entering the rest that has been the sermon's goal since Alma 12.

phrases.term: Abraham paid tithes of one-tenth part of all he possessed
phrases.text: Alma explains his own citation, spelling out that tithes means a tenth. The care suggests hearers who knew the story and perhaps not the arithmetic, and it makes the verse the plainest statement of the principle in the record so far.

phrases.term: He was called the prince of peace
phrases.text: A title Isaiah gives to the Messiah (Isa. 9:6), given here to a king who ended a war in his own city. Alma has spent the chapter saying the order points forward to the Son. The title does the same work in one phrase.

phrases.term: If ye will wrest them it shall be to your own destruction
phrases.text: The end of the doctrinal section, and the tone changes. Alma stops teaching and hands the scriptures over with a warning attached. The destruction is self-inflicted in the grammar as well as the doctrine.

phrases.term: Not procrastinate the day of your repentance
phrases.text: The turn from doctrine to appeal, and Alma prefaces it by naming what it costs him: anxiety unto pain, from the inmost part of his heart. The sermon's most urgent line is also its most personal.

phrases.term: Tempted above that which ye can bear
phrases.text: Paul's promise to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 10:13) in almost the same words, arriving here as an instruction about watching and praying. The Nephite version makes the limit conditional on the watching. The letter does the same, less directly.

verses.label: v. 1–11
verses.title: One noun holds the chapter together
verses.text: Order stands fourteen times across eleven of these verses, always in the same phrase or a variant of it: "the order of his Son," "the holy order of God," "this holy order," "the order of the Son, the Only Begotten of the Father." Manner accompanies it six times, "in what manner to look forward," "this is the manner after which they were ordained," "they were ordained after this manner." The chapter is about a category rather than about people, and it never names a single individual until verse 14.

verses.label: v. 3–5
verses.title: Selection stated, and then its obvious reading blocked
verses.text: The record gives the doctrine with a ground attached: "being called and prepared from the foundation of the world according to the foreknowledge of God, on account of their exceeding faith and good works." The last clause is doing the work, since it makes the calling follow from conduct. Verse 5 then forecloses a reading of privilege before anyone can take it: "in the first place they were on the same standing with their brethren." A record making a claim about foreordination puts the equality clause two verses after it.

verses.label: v. 20
verses.title: A speaker stops and points at a text instead
verses.text: The record has the argument break off in mid-course: "Now I need not rehearse the matter; what I have said may suffice." What replaces further exposition is a reference and a warning: "Behold, the scriptures are before you; if ye will wrest them it shall be to your own destruction." The audience is told the material is available to them and that misreading it is the danger, which shifts the responsibility from the speaker's completeness to the hearer's handling.

verses.label: v. 31
verses.title: A closing admission of omission
verses.text: The chapter ends on the abridger rather than the speaker: "Alma spake many more words unto the people, which are not written in this book." The same formula closes Mosiah 1:8 and appears in a related form at Hel. 8:3 and 3 Ne. 5:8. A chapter that has just told its hearers the scriptures are before them ends by noting that part of what was said is not.

chapter.title: The doctrine of calling is offered to people who denied Alma's
chapter.text: Alma 9:2 had put the objection as a question about credentials, "Who art thou? Suppose ye that we shall believe the testimony of one man?" The answer here never asserts a credential. Verse 3 traces ordination to "exceeding faith and good works" and to being "left to choose good or evil," and verse 5 states the starting position outright, "in the first place they were on the same standing with their brethren." Verse 4 supplies the contrast in the same terms, others rejecting "on account of the hardness of their hearts," so both outcomes are traced to the same origin.

chapter.title: Foreknowledge and choice are held together without resolution
chapter.text: Verse 3 puts preparation before the world and the choosing of good or evil in the same sentence. The chapter never explains how both are true. It refuses to drop either.

chapter.title: The order matters more than the men
chapter.text: Alma moves from the priests to the priesthood in verse 6 and stays there for four verses. What is eternal in this account is the office and its pattern.

chapter.title: Sanctification is described as changed appetite
chapter.text: Not stricter obedience and not a status conferred. The sanctified cannot look at sin without recoiling, which is a claim about desire.

chapter.title: Melchizedek is expanded from three verses to six
chapter.text: The record fills in a figure Genesis barely sketches (Gen. 14:18–20), and what it fills in is a wicked city that repented under one man's preaching. Alma is standing in a wicked city preaching.

chapter.title: The tone breaks at verse 20
chapter.text: Everything before it is exposition. Everything after is voice raised, hand stretched out, and a man naming his own pain. The chapter is built to arrive at the appeal.

chapter.title: The urgency has no date
chapter.text: Alma says the time comes, we know not how soon, and hopes aloud it will be in his day. The pressure in the sermon comes from the hearers' own mortality.

chapter.title: The chapter closes on a gap
chapter.text: Many more words, not written. The record keeps admitting how much it is leaving out, and it does so at the end of its densest teaching on the priesthood.

applications.title: Explain the office instead of defending yourself
applications.text: Accused of overreach at Alma 9:2, Alma taught where authority comes from and then blocked the reading that would have flattered him, "in the first place they were on the same standing with their brethren." When your standing is questioned, describe the thing itself rather than your claim on it.

applications.title: Look at the clause that does the work
applications.text: The calling is "from the foundation of the world according to the foreknowledge of God," and then, "on account of their exceeding faith and good works." The last clause is what makes the doctrine liveable. When a claim about you sounds like destiny, find the part of the sentence that describes conduct.

applications.title: Measure holiness by what repels you
applications.text: The chapter's test is appetite. Notice what you have stopped being able to enjoy over the last few years, and what you have started tolerating. Both directions tell you something.

applications.title: Do the checkable part carefully
applications.text: Alma gives the figure exactly, "tithes of one-tenth part of all he possessed," to hearers who probably knew. Where you are making a large claim, make the small verifiable piece unmistakably clear. It is what buys the rest.

applications.title: Stop and point at the text
applications.text: He breaks off mid-argument, "Now I need not rehearse the matter; what I have said may suffice," and hands over the responsibility, "the scriptures are before you; if ye will wrest them it shall be to your own destruction." Sometimes the useful move is to stop explaining and tell people where to look.

applications.title: Notice the claim about the present
applications.text: Three of the four angel verses speak generally; verse 24 says "angels are declaring it unto many at this time in our land." A doctrine stated in the abstract and a report about this week are different kinds of statement, and it is worth knowing which you have been given.

applications.title: Say what a thing costs you
applications.text: Alma names the anxiety that reaches "pain in my innermost heart" as the reason he keeps pressing. When you have to say something difficult to someone, saying what it costs you is not weakness and it is usually heard.

applications.title: Give the three instructions in order
applications.text: Repent, be humble enough to be led, and then a list: faith, hope, charity, always abounding in good works. The chapter that spends twenty verses on priesthood ends on a set of dispositions any hearer could work on that afternoon.

questions.text: What have I been given that I did not earn, and does knowing that change how I hold it?
Where have I told myself someone else had advantages I lacked, and what would the same story look like told level?
What could I once look at without flinching that I cannot now, and what is the reverse?
What would humbling myself actually consist of this week, in an action someone could observe?
Which passage have I bent to fit a conclusion I had already reached?
What am I putting off that I have already decided is right?
What am I watching and praying about continually, and what am I only remembering when it goes wrong?
